questions.stem: About the Van't Hoff dissociation coefficient α, the correct propositions are:
options: α = number of dissociated moles / initial number of moles
For HCOOH, a weak electrolyte, α = 1
For glucose, α = 1 because all its molecules stay intact
For HCl, a strong electrolyte, α = 1
questions.explanation: α = n(dissociated)/n(initial), so 0 ≤ α ≤ 1. HCl (strong) dissociates completely: α = 1; HCOOH (weak) dissociates partially: α < 1; glucose (non-electrolyte) does not dissociate at all: α = 0, not 1.

questions.stem: Which solute – β pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: β is the number of ions released: Na₂SO₄ → 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻ gives β = 3. NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻ and HCOOH → H⁺ + HCOO⁻ give β = 2; non-electrolytes (urea, glucose) have β = 1, not 0 or 2.

questions.stem: For an aqueous glucose solution of molarity C, the correct propositions are:
options: ω = 0, since glucose does not dissociate
questions.explanation: Glucose is a non-electrolyte: no moles dissociate (α = 0) and β = 1, so ω = [1 + α(β − 1)]C = C. Not dissociating does not make ω zero — each intact molecule still counts as one osmole.

questions.stem: An aqueous solution of formic acid HCOOH (weak electrolyte) at 0.1 mol/L has a dissociation coefficient α = 0.2. Calculate its osmolarity.
questions.explanation: HCOOH → H⁺ + HCOO⁻, β = 2: ω = [1 + 0.2×(2 − 1)]×0.1 = 1.2×0.1 = 0.12 osmol/L. 0.20 assumes total dissociation (strong electrolyte); 0.10 ignores dissociation.

questions.stem: An aqueous Na₂SO₄ solution at 0.2 mol/L has an osmolarity of 0.5 osmol/L. What is its dissociation coefficient α?
questions.explanation: Na₂SO₄ → 2Na⁺ + SO₄²⁻, β = 3: 0.5 = [1 + 2α]×0.2 ⇒ 1 + 2α = 2.5 ⇒ α = 0.75. Using β = 2 gives 1.5, which is impossible since 0 ≤ α ≤ 1.

questions.stem: About osmolarity and osmolality, the correct propositions are:
options: Osmolality is used when the concentration C is expressed as a molality
Molality = number of moles of solute / mass of solvent, expressed in mol/kg
Osmolarity = number of osmoles of solute / volume of solution
Molarity = number of moles of solute / mass of solution
questions.explanation: Osmolarity and molarity are per volume of solution (osmol/L, mol/L); osmolality and molality are per mass of solvent (osmol/kg, mol/kg). The same formula ω = [1 + α(β − 1)]C applies to both.

questions.stem: One liter of aqueous solution contains 0.1 mol of NaCl (totally dissociated) and 0.2 mol of HCOOH (α = 0.1). Calculate the total osmolarity.
questions.explanation: ω = Σ[1 + αᵢ(βᵢ − 1)]Cᵢ: NaCl 2×0.1 = 0.20; HCOOH [1 + 0.1×1]×0.2 = 0.22 ⇒ 0.42 osmol/L. 0.60 treats HCOOH as totally dissociated; 0.40 ignores its dissociation.

questions.stem: In 1 L of water there are 11.7 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) and 9 g of glucose (M = 180 g/mol). NaCl is totally dissociated. Calculate the osmolarity of the solution.
questions.explanation: C(NaCl) = 11.7/58.5 = 0.2 mol/L ⇒ ω = 2×0.2 = 0.4; C(glucose) = 9/180 = 0.05 mol/L ⇒ ω = 0.05 (non-electrolyte). Total 0.45 osmol/L = 450 mosmol/L. 250 forgets NaCl dissociation; 500 doubles glucose.

questions.stem: One liter of aqueous solution contains 14.2 g of Na₂SO₄ (M = 142 g/mol) and 25 mL of H₃PO₄ (2 mol/L). The electrolytes are totally dissociated. Calculate the osmolarity of the solution.
questions.explanation: Na₂SO₄: 0.1 mol/L × β = 3 ⇒ 300 mosm/L. H₃PO₄: 0.025 L × 2 mol/L = 0.05 mol in 1 L, → 3H⁺ + PO₄³⁻ so β = 4 ⇒ 200 mosm/L. Total 500 mosm/L; 450 uses β = 3 for H₃PO₄.

questions.stem: About blood vessels, the correct propositions are:
options: Veins carry blood from the heart to the organs
There are 5 types of blood vessels: arteries, arterioles, capillaries, veins and venules
Gases and nutrients are exchanged between blood and tissues through the capillaries
Gases and nutrients are exchanged between blood and tissues through the arterioles
Arteries carry blood from the heart to the organs
questions.explanation: Blood goes heart → (arteries) → organs → (veins) → heart; exchanges blood ↔ tissues happen across the capillaries, not the arterioles. The 5 vessel types are arteries, arterioles, capillaries, veins and venules.

questions.stem: For a single-solute solution, the osmolarity ω equals the molarity C when:
options: The solute is a strong electrolyte (α = 1)
The solute is NaCl, totally dissociated
The solute is a weak electrolyte (0 < α < 1, β = 2)
questions.explanation: ω = [1 + α(β − 1)]C equals C only when α(β − 1) = 0, i.e. β = 1 (non-electrolyte) or α = 0. Any dissociating electrolyte (α > 0, β ≥ 2) gives ω > C — e.g. totally dissociated NaCl gives ω = 2C.

questions.stem: An aqueous CaCl₂ solution has a molality of 0.3 mol/kg; CaCl₂ is totally dissociated. Its osmolality is:
questions.explanation: CaCl₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻, β = 3, α = 1: ω = 3×0.3 = 0.9. Since C is a molality (mol/kg), ω is an osmolality in osmol/kg, not osmol/L.
